purpose: Structured curriculum payload for the Career Readiness Hub Learn-Apply-Check-Evidence engine.

integration.completionRule: A module is complete when all four stages are completed and evidence is recorded.

learn.objective: Build a repeatable AutoCAD setup that produces clean, reviewable electrical drawings.
learn.seniorReasoning: A senior drafter creates a controlled environment that another designer can understand and safely modify.

apply.scenario: Prepare the drafting setup for a fictional small pump-station electrical floor plan.
tasks: Create a layer plan for equipment, power/cabling, text, dimensions and references.
Define three reusable blocks.
Write five pre-drafting checks.
Record two assumptions requiring design-lead confirmation.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized setup sheet or screenshot set with layer structure, sample blocks and pre-drafting checklist.

questions.prompt: Two designers use different layer conventions on one package. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Agree a package standard, update the controlled template/standards and check affected sheets for consistency.

questions.prompt: What should be confirmed before creating a reusable block?
questions.answer: Project standard, insertion behaviour, attributes and intended reuse across the package.

questions.prompt: What demonstrates senior ownership before drafting starts?
questions.answer: Identify inputs, interfaces, assumptions and approval boundaries that could change the drawing.

evidence.prompt: Capture one sanitized artefact or written record proving you can establish a controlled drafting setup and explain the decisions behind it.

learn.objective: Use MicroStation CONNECT with disciplined level structures, references, annotation and production controls.
learn.seniorReasoning: The goal is not merely knowing commands; it is being able to structure a DGN so the package remains understandable, coordinated and maintainable.

apply.scenario: Set up a fictional electrical switchroom drawing in MicroStation CONNECT using a controlled level and reference strategy.
tasks: Define a level naming structure for equipment, power, containment, text, dimensions and references.
Attach a fictional architectural reference and describe its update implications.
Create representative electrical annotation and verify element attributes.
Document three checks before issue.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized DGN screenshots or a written production record showing level structure, references, annotation and QA checks.

questions.prompt: A reference file changes after you have started drafting. What should a senior designer consider first?
questions.answer: Assess the reference revision/change, identify affected geometry and interfaces, then coordinate the impact before blindly updating the drawing.

questions.prompt: Why is a controlled level structure important?
questions.answer: It makes graphics predictable, supports review/filtering and reduces coordination and editing errors.

questions.prompt: What is stronger than checking only whether a sheet looks correct?
questions.answer: Check model structure, references, attributes, annotation, standards and issue information as well as appearance.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized MicroStation production example demonstrating controlled levels, references, annotation and a documented QA check.

learn.objective: Move from drawing production to controlled ownership of an electrical drawing through review, coordination and issue.
learn.seniorReasoning: Ownership means understanding what the drawing communicates, what inputs it depends on, what changed and what must be checked before issue.

apply.scenario: Review a fictional electrical drawing package containing a redline, a changed equipment location and an interface with mechanical services.
tasks: Classify each redline as drafting correction, design decision, coordination issue or clarification.
Identify missing inputs before incorporating the change.
Update a revision/disposition record.
Perform a structured self-check before issue.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized redline disposition table plus a drawing QA checklist and short issue-readiness statement.

questions.prompt: A redline changes equipment location but the upstream cable route may be affected. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Do not treat it as an isolated drafting edit; identify affected interfaces and verify electrical consequences before issue.

questions.prompt: When should a drafter escalate rather than make an assumption?
questions.answer: When the change affects design intent, safety, compliance, interfaces or an approval boundary that has not been defined.

questions.prompt: What makes a QA check senior-level?
questions.answer: It checks drawing correctness plus information, interfaces, revision status and design assumptions before issue.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized redline/disposition exercise and QA record demonstrating controlled drawing ownership.

learn.objective: Read and produce clear electrical single-line diagrams while maintaining traceability between equipment, protection, conductors and downstream loads.
learn.seniorReasoning: An SLD is a controlled representation of the electrical system. Major elements need a reason, an identifiable relationship to other documents and enough information for review.

apply.scenario: Develop a fictional SLD for a small pump-station distribution system supplied from an LV switchboard through a motor-control section to two pumps and auxiliary loads.
tasks: Establish source-to-load hierarchy and equipment tags.
Represent incomer, protection, feeders, motor starters/VSD interfaces and outgoing loads.
Create a feeder identification scheme and avoid duplicating controlled schedule data.
Cross-check against a fictional equipment list and identify three discrepancies.
Prepare an issue-readiness checklist.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized SLD exercise plus discrepancy/assumption register and issue-readiness checklist.

questions.prompt: An equipment tag appears on the SLD but not in the equipment list. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Treat it as a coordination discrepancy, trace the source and confirm the intended equipment before issuing rather than silently creating or deleting information.

questions.prompt: Why should detailed cable schedule data not simply be copied in full onto every SLD?
questions.answer: The SLD should communicate system relationships and key design information while detailed cable data remains controlled in its schedule; duplication increases inconsistency risk.

questions.prompt: A protective device rating changes. What should be checked beyond changing the number on the SLD?
questions.answer: Check affected feeder/cable information, equipment interfaces, schedules, downstream loads, coordination assumptions and revision impacts.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized SLD exercise and supporting discrepancy/QA record demonstrating system-documentation capability.
criteria: Equipment and feeder identifiers are traceable

learn.objective: Create and review cable schedules and termination information as controlled design records with traceability from source equipment through destination and termination.
learn.seniorReasoning: Senior ownership means maintaining traceability across documents and identifying discrepancies before they become construction or commissioning problems.

apply.scenario: Build a fictional pump-station cable package with a motor-control panel, two pumps, local isolators and control interfaces; include two intentional tag mismatches and incomplete inputs.
tasks: Create at least eight fictional power, control and indication cables.
Record source, destination, tag, service, core requirement and reference.
Flag tag mismatches and identify controlled sources to verify.
Create a termination checklist.
Classify at least three assumptions or missing inputs as acceptable, clarification or blocking.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized cable schedule plus termination/checking checklist and discrepancy register.

questions.prompt: A cable tag conflicts between the equipment list and SLD. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Record the discrepancy, trace both sources, identify the controlled source or obtain clarification before issuing the affected information.

questions.prompt: Which combination gives the strongest cable traceability?
questions.answer: Source, destination, cable tag, service and linked drawing/reference information.

questions.prompt: An important termination detail is missing. What should you do?
questions.answer: Identify the missing input, state its impact and obtain the required information before the affected deliverable is issued.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized cable schedule, termination checklist or discrepancy register demonstrating controlled documentation and traceability.
criteria: Assumptions and missing inputs are visible
A cross-document QA check is documented
Learner explains what the evidence proves

modules.title: AS/NZS 3000 Wiring Rules — Structure and Application

learn.objective: Build a disciplined workflow for locating, interpreting and applying AS/NZS 3000 requirements without treating standards as a substitute for engineering judgement.
learn.seniorReasoning: A senior designer records the requirement being applied, checks scope and project context, and escalates interpretations that exceed the role or available design basis.

apply.scenario: Review a fictional LV pump-station arrangement and identify where standards checks are required before drawing issue.
tasks: Create a standards lookup log with clause/topic, design question and outcome.
Identify protection, segregation, wiring-method and accessibility checks relevant to the scenario.
Separate confirmed requirements from items requiring engineer interpretation.
Record three design-basis questions that would block issue if unanswered.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized standards application checklist and lookup log.

questions.prompt: You find a clause that appears relevant but the project scope is unclear. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Confirm the clause scope and project applicability before applying it, and escalate any interpretation that affects design intent or compliance.

questions.prompt: What makes a standards reference useful in a drawing review?
questions.answer: It links the requirement to a specific design decision, check or documented assumption rather than merely listing a standard number.

questions.prompt: When should standards research be escalated?
questions.answer: When the requirement is ambiguous, affects safety/compliance, or requires engineering judgement beyond the defined responsibility.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized standards lookup/checklist demonstrating disciplined AS/NZS application and escalation awareness.

modules.title: Owning a Drawing Package End to End

learn.objective: Control an electrical drawing package from inputs and coordination through checking, revision and issue.
learn.seniorReasoning: Ownership is demonstrated by controlling the information flow, not merely completing individual drawings.

apply.scenario: Plan a fictional five-drawing electrical package with architectural, mechanical and vendor interfaces and one late design change.
tasks: Create an input and interface register.
Map dependencies between drawings, schedules and references.
Create a revision/change-impact record.
Run a package-level QA review and identify blockers.
Write an issue recommendation with open actions.
apply.deliverable: Package control sheet, interface register, change-impact record and QA checklist.

questions.prompt: A late vendor change affects two drawings and a cable schedule. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Trace the change across all affected deliverables, update controlled records, coordinate dependencies and re-check before issue.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an input register?
questions.answer: To make required information, status, ownership and missing inputs visible so package progress is controlled.

questions.prompt: When should a package be held from issue?
questions.answer: When unresolved changes or missing inputs can affect design intent, safety, compliance, coordination or traceability.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized package-control exercise showing end-to-end drawing ownership.

learn.objective: Develop a controlled workflow for arranging a power distribution board while considering equipment, access, containment, cable entry and documentation interfaces.
learn.seniorReasoning: A good layout is not just visually tidy; it must support installation, maintenance, cable routing and coordinated documentation.

apply.scenario: Lay out a fictional LV distribution board serving pumps, small power and control auxiliaries.
tasks: Establish incomer and outgoing arrangement logic.
Reserve space for devices, terminals and cable entry.
Identify maintainability and access considerations.
Cross-check board tags and outgoing circuits against an SLD.
Record layout assumptions requiring vendor or engineer confirmation.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized board GA sketch plus layout checklist and discrepancy register.

questions.prompt: A board layout fits all devices but leaves poor cable-entry access. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Treat cable entry and maintainability as design constraints, revise the arrangement and coordinate the impact rather than accepting a merely fitting layout.

questions.prompt: Why should a board GA be cross-checked against the SLD?
questions.answer: To confirm device identities, circuit relationships, ratings/labels and outgoing references remain consistent across documents.

questions.prompt: What should be recorded when vendor dimensions are unavailable?
questions.answer: The assumption, its basis, its impact and the confirmation required before the layout becomes issue-ready.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized distribution-board layout and coordination record demonstrating practical layout ownership.

learn.objective: Understand and document the cable-sizing workflow, inputs and checks needed before relying on a cable selection.
learn.seniorReasoning: The senior skill is controlling the calculation inputs and knowing when a result requires engineering review, not guessing a cable size.

apply.scenario: Review a fictional three-phase motor feeder and prepare a calculation-input sheet and high-level sizing check.
tasks: Record load, supply, route, installation and environmental inputs.
Identify the relevant capacity and voltage-drop checks.
Document assumptions and missing inputs.
Compare a proposed cable selection against the required checks.
Write a concise engineering-review handover.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized calculation-input sheet, high-level check and review handover.

questions.prompt: A proposed cable passes a simple voltage-drop check but installation details are unknown. What is the strongest response?
questions.answer: Do not treat the result as final; confirm installation method and other capacity/derating inputs before accepting the selection.

questions.prompt: Why is the calculation input record important?
questions.answer: It makes the basis, assumptions and missing information traceable so another engineer can verify the result.

questions.prompt: When should cable sizing be escalated?
questions.answer: When critical inputs are missing, the result affects compliance/safety, or engineering judgement is required for the selection.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized cable-sizing workflow record demonstrating controlled inputs, checks and engineering handover.

learn.objective: Understand the purpose of protection coordination and how a designer should recognize discrimination, protection and fault-level interfaces.
learn.seniorReasoning: The senior designer recognizes protection dependencies and avoids presenting a coordination outcome without the required engineering basis.

apply.scenario: Review a fictional LV feeder with upstream and downstream protective devices and identify coordination questions before drawing issue.
tasks: Map upstream/downstream device relationships.
Identify required fault-level and device data.
Record which coordination questions need calculation or engineer confirmation.
Check protection references on an SLD and equipment schedule.
Prepare a protection-review action list.
apply.deliverable: Sanitized protection coordination review sheet and action list.

questions.prompt: A downstream breaker rating changes. What is the strongest senior response?
questions.answer: Assess the upstream/downstream relationship and coordination impact using the required engineering data before accepting the change.

questions.prompt: Why is fault-level information important to protection review?
questions.answer: Protection device capability and coordination depend on the available fault conditions and selected device characteristics.

questions.prompt: What should a drafter avoid claiming without the engineering basis?
questions.answer: A definitive discrimination or protection-coordination result when the required calculations, device data or settings have not been verified.

evidence.prompt: Capture a sanitized protection review showing device relationships, required inputs and engineering-review boundaries.
